items.title: [envd] envd: Host file disclosure through requirements path traversal and TOCTOU
items.summary: Summaryenvd’s install.python_packages(requirements=...) could read files outside the build context on the host. Content interpreted as dependency entries could appear in build logs and build-step metadata.Commit f576c92, released in v1.3.5, added path containment validation but left a time-of-check/time-of-use (TOCTOU) race between symlink resolution and opening the requirements file. Commit 9d575b3 addresses this race by opening requirements files through a directory-rooted filesystem handle.Detailsenvd reads requirements files on the host to determine whether their contents can be embedded directly into a pip installation build step.The vulnerable host-side requirements read was introduced in v0.3.38. Version v1.3.5 added containment checks for static path escapes but remained vulnerable to a TOCTOU race. The complete fix is included in v1.3.6.Before f576c92, this host read lacked a build-context containment check. That commit added frontend path validation and a compile-time check using filepath.EvalSymlinks followed by a containment comparison.However, symlink resolution returns a pathname rather than a pinned filesystem object. The subsequent os.Open independently resolves that pathname. Concurrent filesystem changes could therefore invalidate the containment check before the file was opened.The complete fix uses os.OpenRoot and Root.Open to enforce containment during filesystem traversal.Resources:first commit: be783264fdd79ad7262cea0485b7d449ca514f80Initial containment fix: f576c92TOCTOU fix: 9d575b3Proof of conceptThe security-relevant condition is a requirements-file pathname whose filesystem resolution changes between validation and opening. The containment check describes the filesystem at validation time, while the later pathname-based open may access a different object.The fix includes a deterministic regression test for the underlying object-pinning guarantee. It opens a context directory handle, moves that directory, and creates a replacement directory at the original pathname containing different requirements. The rooted reader continues reading the original context; a pathname-based reader reads the replacement.This regression test demonstrates the distinction between rooted and pathname-based reads. It is not an end-to-end demonstration of host file disclosure.ImpactAn attacker who can influence the build input—and, for the residual race in v1.3.5, concurrently modify the relevant filesystem paths—may cause envd to read files outside the intended build context, subject to the permissions of the envd process.Depending on the file contents and requirements parsing, information may be exposed through dependency debug logs and build-step metadata. This issue does not establish arbitrary code execution or unrestricted disclosure of every file.v1.3.5 remains affected by the TOCTOU variant. Earlier versions containing the host requirements-reading behavior are affected by the original containment issue; confirm the earliest affected release before setting the advisory’s version range.Patched version: v1.3.6.Referenceshttps://github.com/tensorchord/envd/security/advisories/GHSA-jv6m-48w5-5rprhttps://github.com/tensorchord/envd/pull/2112https://github.com/tensorchord/envd/pull/2119https://github.com/tensorchord/envd/commit/9d575b354ce17a02ef9698b6ff0d5d14296c5734https://github.com/tensorchord/envd/commit/f576c92c1e6dcb9b00b60995534aeb2a83b0b407https://github.com/tensorchord/envd/releases/tag/v1.3.6https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jv6m-48w5-5rpr

items.title: [opentelemetry-api] OpenTelemetry Python API: Denial of service through quadratic-time traceparent parsing
items.summary: SummaryTraceContextTextMapPropagator.extract() in opentelemetry-api is vulnerable to regular expression denial of service (ReDoS) when processing a specially crafted traceparent value.A malformed value containing a trace-context prefix followed by a long whitespace sequence and an embedded newline triggers quadratic-time regex backtracking. Applications that extract trace context from untrusted carriers accepting such strings can experience excessive CPU consumption and request-processing delays.When extraction runs on an asynchronous server’s event-loop thread, a single malicious message can delay unrelated requests handled by that event loop.Exposure conditionsExploitation requires attacker-controlled input to reach the affected propagator through a carrier that preserves embedded newlines and permits a sufficiently large value.Conforming HTTP header values cannot contain embedded newlines. However, OpenTelemetry carriers are not restricted to HTTP headers. JSON strings can contain escaped newlines that become newline characters after decoding.MCP request metadata is one relevant integration path: applications may extract trace context from JSON params._meta. Exposure depends on the MCP SDK or instrumentation version, whether extraction invokes the W3C Trace Context propagator, and applicable message-size limits. HTTP header validation does not constrain a traceparent string carried inside a JSON body.Authentication requirements depend on the application exposing the carrier.ImpactThe demonstrated impact is denial of service through excessive CPU consumption and blocked request processing. Repeated malicious messages may sustain service degradation.This finding does not demonstrate data disclosure, data modification, or code execution.RemediationUpgrade opentelemetry-api to 1.45.2 or a later release containing the fix.Version 1.45.2 rejects traceparent values longer than 512 characters before regex matching and removes the overlapping suffix and trailing-whitespace expressions.Where upgrading is temporarily unavailable, reject oversized values and embedded CR/LF characters before passing untrusted trace-context values to the affected propagator.Referenceshttps://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-python/security/advisories/GHSA-mf5v-w3w3-f6cghttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-126360https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-python/pull/5818https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-python/pull/5856https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-python/commit/78123a2755c907c602e02352aebed4be86aa5350https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-python/commit/faa72dae511ae64a7bf8ca63eff9ad4387d0b939https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-python/releases/tag/v1.45.2https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mf5v-w3w3-f6cg

items.title: [soupsieve] Soup Sieve: Exponential ReDoS in selector compilation via \9-run in CSS_ESCAPES/IDENTIFIER
items.summary: SummaryThe IDENTIFIER/CSS_ESCAPES regex (css_parser.py:119-124) exhibits exponential backtracking on a run of ambiguous digit-escapes (\9) in an attribute-name or tag position of an otherwise well-formed selector. It fires at compile time (before the SELECTOR_LIMIT guard) via the public soupsieve.compile() and BeautifulSoup .select().PoC (verified on soupsieve 2.9.2)import soupsieve as svsv.compile('[a' + '\\9'*26 + '=x]')   # ~57 bytes -> ~10s; ~16x time per +4 charsNoveltyDistinct from the patched GHSA-836r-... (VALUE regex) and GHSA-2wc2-... (comma-list) advisories, which are fixed in 2.9.2; this is a different regex/vector.ReachabilityCSS selectors are usually developer-controlled, so exposure requires an application that compiles UNTRUSTED selector strings (web-scraping-as-a-service, no-code/query builders, user-defined extraction rules). Where selectors are user-supplied, a ~60-byte string hangs the worker.NoteThis issue was fixed in version 3.0.0, which has been yanked from the PyPI registry. Use versions 3.0.2 and above to upgrade.Referenceshttps://github.com/facelessuser/soupsieve/security/advisories/GHSA-6655-6qjp-jx7xhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-126191https://github.com/facelessuser/soupsieve/pull/300https://github.com/facelessuser/soupsieve/commit/dbfa2854ff31a863326bd6660d4e55c6f068db9ehttps://github.com/facelessuser/soupsieve/releases/tag/3.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6655-6qjp-jx7x

items.title: [soupsieve] Soup Sieve: Uncontrolled recursion in CSS parser lets nested pseudo-class selectors exhaust the Python call stack
items.summary: SummaryThe Soup Sieve CSS selector parser recurses once per level of nested pseudo-class selector (:is(), :not(), :where(), :has()) without any limit on nesting depth. An unauthenticated attacker who can supply a CSS selector string to soupsieve.compile(), soupsieve.select(), or Beautiful Soup's soup.select() / soup.select_one() can force the parser to exceed Python's recursion limit with a small crafted input (about 1.6 KB, roughly 330 nesting levels), raising an uncontrolled RecursionError. Because this exception is not part of the parser's documented error contract, applications that catch only ValueError or SelectorSyntaxError see an unexpected failure of the request or task that parsed the selector.Root CauseThe parser dispatches each opening pseudo-class token to parse_pseudo_open, which calls back into parse_selectors to parse the pseudo-class body. Every nesting level therefore adds Python stack frames, and no counter, depth guard, or RecursionError handler bounds this descent. The token-count guard SELECTOR_LIMIT = 8192 (added for the earlier comma-separated-list memory issue) counts parsed tokens, not recursion depth; at the failing nesting depth the token count is only about 330, roughly four percent of that limit, so the guard never fires. The security invariant that untrusted selector input must not be able to exhaust interpreter resources is not enforced for nesting depth.soupsieve/css_parser.py  CSSParser.parse_pseudo_open (line 985): sel.selectors.append(self.parse_selectors(iselector, index, flags))  CSSParser.parse_selectors  (line 1137): recursive target; dispatches pseudo-class tokens back into parse_pseudo_class -> parse_pseudo_open  CSSParser.increment_count  (lines 707-712): SELECTOR_LIMIT token guard; increments once per nesting level, cannot bound depthImpactAny application that compiles or evaluates untrusted CSS selectors through Soup Sieve (directly or via Beautiful Soup) is affected. No authentication, privilege, or user interaction is required; the failure occurs during selector parsing, before any document is matched. A single crafted selector of about 1.6 KB reliably raises RecursionError. The demonstrated capability is a transient denial of the individual request, task, or invocation that parsed the malicious selector: the exception propagates uncaught unless the caller handles RecursionError (or a broad except Exception). The RecursionError in CPython 3.x is a recoverable stack unwind, not an interpreter crash or persistent resource exhaustion, and it carries no confidentiality or integrity impact. Applications following the parser's documented error pattern (catching ValueError / SelectorSyntaxError) will not catch it, so a repeated stream of such selectors can plausibly cause repeated per-request failures; this per-request availability effect is the demonstrated consequence, not a service-wide or amplified outage.Proof of ConceptRequires only an installed Soup Sieve (any release from 0.4 through 2.10) and a default CPython recursion limit of 1000. No Beautiful Soup document or network setup is needed.import soupsieve as sv# ~330 levels of nested :is() around a single tag: about 1.6 KB of input.depth = 330selector = ":is(" * depth + "a" + ")" * depthprint("selector length:", len(selector))sv.compile(selector)selector length: 1651Traceback (most recent call last):  ...  File ".../soupsieve/css_parser.py", line 985, in parse_pseudo_open    sel.selectors.append(self.parse_selectors(iselector, index, flags))RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceededThe same failure was reproduced with :not(), :where(), and :has(), and through BeautifulSoup(...).select(selector). A negative control at depth 100 compiles successfully with a token count of 101, confirming the token guard is far from firing.Attack ChainExposure: The application exposes soupsieve.compile() / select() or Beautiful Soup's .select() / .select_one() to attacker-influenced CSS selector input. These are the library's primary public API and ship enabled by default; Soup Sieve is an automatic dependency of Beautiful Soup 4.Control: The attacker fully controls the selector string. The nested pseudo-class pattern (:is(:is(...a...))) survives tokenization and normalization unchanged.Path: compile() reaches CSSParser.process_selectors() and then parse_selectors(), which dispatches each pseudo-class token through parse_pseudo_class() into parse_pseudo_open(), which calls parse_selectors() again, once per nesting level.Guard: The only resource guard is the SELECTOR_LIMIT token counter, which reaches about 330 at the failing depth versus its limit of 8192, so it never fires. No recursion-depth counter and no RecursionError handler exist anywhere in the package.Primitive: Python's recursion limit is exceeded during parsing, raising an uncontrolled RecursionError.Result: The unhandled RecursionError propagates to the caller, failing the request, task, or process invocation that parsed the selector, outside the parser's docume
